analysis.one_liner: Caps jury awards against negligent doctors, drug makers, and corporations and restricts injured people's lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on January 21, 1997 and never received a hearing, amendment, or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite civil lawsuit rules across federal and state courts. It would cap "pain and suffering" awards against doctors, hospitals, and health plans at $250,000, bar punitive damages against drug and device makers whose products the FDA approved, cap punitive damages in all cases at the greater of three times actual losses or $250,000, end joint liability for pain-and-suffering awards, impose a two-year deadline for malpractice suits, tighten the rules for expert witnesses, and let defendants who offer a settlement collect their legal fees from losing plaintiffs who rejected it. It was introduced by the chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, but the committee never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Defendants in injury lawsuits: medical malpractice insurers, hospitals, managed care companies, physicians, brand-name drug and medical device manufacturers, and businesses generally. They gain because the most unpredictable parts of jury awards — punitive damages and large pain-and-suffering verdicts — would be capped or barred, and lawsuits would face shorter deadlines and new cost risks for plaintiffs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurers, drug makers, hospitals, large businesses

how_it_helps.text: Caps noneconomic (pain-and-suffering) damages in any health care liability suit at $250,000 no matter how many parties or claims are involved, and keeps the jury from being told about the cap [S2, S3].

Bars punitive damages against a drug or medical device manufacturer whose product received FDA premarket approval or is generally recognized as safe and effective, unless the company withheld or misrepresented material information to the FDA or bribed an FDA official [S3].

Limits punitive damages in all civil cases to conduct intended to harm or showing conscious, flagrant disregard, proven by clear and convincing evidence, and caps awards at the greater of three times economic damages or $250,000 [S2, S3].

Prohibits any second punitive damages award against a defendant for the same act or course of conduct in any later state or federal lawsuit, with only narrow exceptions for newly discovered wrongdoing [S2, S3].
Ends joint liability for noneconomic damages, so each defendant pays only its own percentage share of pain-and-suffering awards [S2, S3].

Sets a two-year deadline (six-year outside limit) for filing a health care liability action, and lets defendants pay large future damage awards in periodic installments that end if the injured person dies or returns to work [S2, S3].

Rewrites Federal Rules of Evidence and Civil Procedure to tighten admissibility of expert testimony and to require a plaintiff who rejects a settlement offer and then does no better at trial to pay the defendant's costs and attorney fees [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured by medical negligence, defective drugs, unsafe devices, and other wrongdoing. A child with a lifetime of injuries from a doctor's error could recover no more than $250,000 for pain and suffering, however severe the harm; a suit filed more than two years after an injury was discovered would be barred; punitive punishment of a reckless but FDA-approved drug maker would be off the table; and a plaintiff who turns down a low settlement offer and wins less at trial could owe the defendant's legal bills. The bill itself does not say who would make up the difference.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap applies regardless of how catastrophic the injury is, and the jury is never told the cap exists — the award is silently cut after the verdict [S3].

The two-year filing deadline with a six-year outside limit could cut off malpractice claims discovered late, and periodic payment awards terminate if the injured person dies or returns to work, leaving nothing for dependents beyond a duty-of-support carve-out [S3].

Ending joint liability means an injured person who proves harm but cannot collect from the main wrongdoer — for example, an insolvent or judgment-proof defendant — absorbs the unpaid share of the award [S3].

The rewritten settlement rule requires a losing plaintiff who rejected an offer to pay the defendant's costs and reasonable attorney fees, which could deter smaller claims from being brought at all [S3].

The bill preempts state law: states whose own tort systems already balance these questions, including some that allow higher or unlimited awards, would have their rules overridden in these areas [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's sponsors argued that unpredictable jury awards raise everyone's costs and that repeated punitive awards punish defendants twice for the same conduct [S3]. Those are real concerns, and limiting duplicate punitive awards has some due-process logic. But the bill's largest provisions do not just discipline outliers — they systematically shift risk away from defendants and onto the people least able to bear it: a fixed $250,000 cap on the most severe injuries, a shortened filing window, and fee-shifting that punishes plaintiffs for miscalculating a settlement. On balance, the consumer cost outweighs the efficiency gain, particularly in the health care title.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch introduced the Civil Justice Fairness Act of 1997 on January 21, 1997, joined by Senators Kyl and Thomas [S1, S3, S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House companion action before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].
The bill's two cosponsors were both Republicans; it attracted no Democratic support on the record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People injured by medical malpractice and defective products kept the legal remedies they had, since the caps, deadlines, and FDA liability shield were never enacted. Defendant industries and insurers would have gained if it had passed, but it never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured people, who kept existing remedies

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans and both cosponsors were Republicans; the bill never reached a vote, so no record shows how the full chamber or any opponents would have split.

industries.note: The bill caps the largest component of malpractice payouts — pain-and-suffering awards — at $250,000, shortens the filing window, and lets insurers pay large judgments in installments that can end early. Its gains come directly out of the compensation injured patients would otherwise receive.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug and medical device makers
industries.note: Punitive damages would be barred against makers of FDA-approved drugs and devices, with a narrow exception for companies that deceived or bribed the FDA. This would shield companies from the main financial penalty for marketing a dangerous product the agency approved.

industries.industry: Hospitals, managed care companies, and physicians
industries.note: The health care title caps noneconomic damages and covers health plans themselves, including entities obligated to pay for care. Every dollar of capped or eliminated recovery is a cost avoided by providers and insurers and a loss borne by the injured patient.

industries.industry: Large businesses and corporate defendants generally
industries.note: Across all civil cases, punitive awards would be capped, easier to bifurcate at a defendant's request, unavailable after a first award for the same conduct, and subject to new expert-testimony and settlement cost-shifting rules that raise the risk of suing. The bill's own findings name businesses as the intended beneficiaries.

The bill requires disclosure of hours and referral fees in contingency arrangements and directs the Attorney General to study fee 'abuses' and draft model state legislation. Their financial interest runs with their clients': lower awards and fee-shifting shrink the cases lawyers can afford to take for injured people who cannot pay hourly rates.
